newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Small caps still awaiting January boost.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Small caps still awaiting January boost.

text.p: More than midway through what is annually one of their best months, small cap stocks show few signs their seasonal rally is at hand -- a fact analysts said bodes ill for the entire market.
The start of the year traditionally finds the market flush with retirement account cash. This year, that cash has fueled the Dow Industrials' relentless run towards 7000.
But many eyes are on the background, where a quiet Russell 2000 index has labored to overcome last summer's sell-off.
Willingness to embrace small cap stocks is viewed as an important barometer of investor confidence. For now, buying interest rests firmly with large cap, highly-liquid issues.
There are two reasons now is considered a critical time for small caps to assert themselves.

One is the "January effect," which refers to the small cap rally that often occurs as fund managers, flush with retirement account cash, pluck up low-priced bargains created by December tax-loss selling.
Instead, buying has been concentrated on the large cap names, which could be an ill omen.

"A handful of primary technology and big cap stocks, even in the OTC market, have been driving the indexes," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "We really haven't seen a big push in small caps so we are not getting that real January effect."
"We should know by the middle of next month," Harrington said. "If (small cap stocks) don't pick up by then, we could be hitting a correction."
The second is that the Russell 2000 small cap index has just recently edged to record territory, some eight months after its last peak.
The index was particularly hard hit in July, bottoming almost 15 percent below its May highs.
It was not until January 7 that the index recouped its losses and by last Friday's close the Russell stood at 367.88, for a paltry one percent gain in eight months.
In contrast, the Dow industrials were back in record territory by September, staged a furious rally in November and have added six percent in new gains since the year started.
What happens to the Russell in the next few weeks is critical, analysts said.

"I would look at the oscillators (a measure of momentum) in the index. It would be negative if the index was making new highs and the oscillators lower peaks but I don't see that now," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co. "We need time -- I'd say about a month -- to bear this out."

Because the small cap universe is so diverse, analysts use a host of indicators to gauge sentiment and strength. Even so, they say the Russell offers the simplest snapshot of small caps, much in the way the Standard & Poor's 500 index offers a quick, fairly comprehensive look at large caps.
Using the Russell snapshot, analysts saw little evidence of an imminent small-cap rally.

"I've seen no signs yet that the Russell is going to start outperforming," said Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst, at Raymond, James and Associates. "I've been hearing it was about to come for four or five months now and it hasn't happened."
Another reason for analysts' concern is that overall overall market peaks tend to be preceded by small-cap peaks and the Russell's recent foray into record ground has been unconvincing.

"The Russell has been underperforming since the end of December," said Green said. "If it doesn't follow through on this rally, a lot of people will be disappointed, sensing this will be last phase of this bull market."
If their fortunes do turn around, the small caps will have to surmount the skepticism of not only individual investors, but also some of the professionals who advise them.
"Ninety percent of the time I tend to recommend and trade large caps," Bloch said. "I tell our brokers, 'Don't even call me asking for an opinion on a stock that's $5 or less.'"
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
